name: BUF602IDBVT
title: 1000 MHz closed-loop unity-gain buffer with mid-supply reference
summary: The BUF602 is a wideband closed-loop buffer with a gain of one: 1000 MHz small-signal bandwidth and 8000 V/µs slew rate on ±5 V, from 5.8 mA. It runs from ±1.4 V to ±6.3 V or +2.8 V to +12.6 V, drives 60 mA continuously and 350 mA peak, and has an extra buffered mid-supply reference output (VREF) for biasing AC-coupled single-supply circuits. It comes in SO-8 and SOT23-5.

circuits.title: Self-referenced, AC-coupled, single-supply buffer
circuits.description: A single-supply AC buffer that biases its own input. The signal comes in through a coupling capacitor; a 2 kΩ resistor ties the input pin to the VREF pin, which sits at VCC/2, and 1 µF from VREF to ground quiets the reference. The input looks like about 2 kΩ to the source and the output impedance stays under 2 Ω up to 20 MHz.

parts.note: input coupling capacitor; no value given

notes: Input impedance ≈ 2 kΩ; output impedance ZO < 2 Ω to 20 MHz.

circuits.title: DC-coupled, bipolar-supply specification and test circuit
circuits.description: The ±5 V test set-up. A 50 Ω resistor to ground terminates the 50 Ω source at the input pin; a 50 Ω series resistor at the output feeds a 50 Ω load. Each supply pin has 0.1 µF and 4.7 µF to ground. VREF is left open.
notes: Voltage swings in the electrical tables are measured right at the In and Out pins; powers in dBm are at the matched 50 Ω load.
A 0.01 µF capacitor added between the two supply pins typically improves 2nd-harmonic distortion by 3 dB to 6 dB.

circuits.title: AC-coupled, single-supply specification and test circuit
circuits.description: The +5 V test set-up. The 50 Ω-terminated input is AC-coupled through 0.1 µF into the input pin, which a 2 kΩ resistor biases from the VREF pin; 0.1 µF from VREF to ground filters the reference. The output drives a 50 Ω series resistor into a 50 Ω load returned to VCC/2, 100 Ω in all.

circuits.title: Line driver
circuits.description: The buffer drives a transmission line of impedance ZO through a series resistor ROUT; RLOAD to ground terminates the far end, where VOUT is taken. The buffer offers a high input impedance and a low output impedance.
notes: J3 and J4 are the supply connections.

circuits.title: Self-biased, low-impedance mid-supply voltage reference
circuits.description: The part buffers its own mid-supply reference. VREF carries 0.1 µF to ground to filter the divider's noise and feeds the input pin through 20 Ω; the output then holds VS/2 at low impedance from DC to 250 MHz.

where.VREFL: part of VOUT reflected back from the far end

equations.name: Reflection factor
equations.note: Γ runs from –1 to +1: ZO = Z1 gives Γ = 0 and VREFL = 0; ZO = ∞ gives Γ = –1 and VREFL = –VOUT; ZO = 0 gives Γ = +1 and VREFL = +VOUT. Misprint: shown under a square root; it should read Γ = (Z1 − ZO) / (Z1 + ZO).

where.PDQ: quiescent power: total voltage across the part multiplied by its unloaded supply current
where.PDL: extra dissipation in the output transistors while they supply the load

equations.name: Worst-case output-stage dissipation
equations.note: For equal bipolar supplies and a grounded resistive load, PDL peaks when the output sits at half of either supply. Example, BUF602IDBV at +85 °C driving 20 Ω: PD = 10 V × 5.8 mA + 5²/(4 × 20 Ω) = 370.5 mW; maximum TJ = +85 °C + (0.37 W × 150 °C/W) = 141 °C.

operation.text: A closed-loop, unity-gain wideband buffer with a second, separate unity-gain buffer for a mid-supply reference. Two internal 50 kΩ resistors split the supply; that buffer drives the VREF pin through 200 Ω. AC-coupled designs can bias the input from VREF and save external parts and supply current.

On 5.8 mA of quiescent current the output gets within about 1 V of either rail and delivers more than 60 mA at room temperature, and the bias does not depend on the supply voltage. On a single +5 V supply it gives over 500 MHz of bandwidth at 2 VPP into 100 Ω, and a 3 VPP swing with over 400 MHz. The output does not reach the rails: single-supply designs keep the signal inside the usable swing, for instance by AC-coupling it onto the VREF bias.

With no load at +25 °C the output typically comes closer than 1.2 V to either rail, and the +25 °C limit is 1.2 V from either rail. Into 15 Ω, the smallest tested load, it delivers more than ±60 mA. The voltage-current limit plot is bounded by 1 W of internal dissipation; its load lines show ±3 V into 25 Ω and ±3.5 V into 50 Ω within both the output limits and the 1 W limit. The over-temperature output limits are worst-case simulations at the cold end; once the output transistors warm up, the available swing and current rise above them.

Heavy output power can call for a heat sink or forced air. What heats the die is the power lost in the output transistors, not the power reaching the load. The worst case is a load that forces current into the output at positive output voltages or draws it out at negative ones, putting large current across a large internal drop.

The reference output yields a stiff half-supply voltage when buffered by the part itself (DC to 250 MHz with 0.1 µF on VREF). A capacitor on VREF is recommended to limit the bandwidth of the noise from the two internal 50 kΩ divider resistors.

Besides the usual capacitors from each supply to ground, a 0.01 µF capacitor between the two supply pins typically improves 2nd-harmonic distortion by 3 dB to 6 dB (with bipolar supplies, 0.1 µF across them improves it as well). The 0.1 µF high-frequency capacitors go within 0.25 inch of the supply pins with wide, short traces; larger 2.2 µF to 6.8 µF capacitors on the main supply pins can sit farther away and serve several parts.

Keep stray capacitance to AC ground off the signal pins: cut back every ground and power plane under and around the In and Out pins and leave the planes whole elsewhere. Stray capacitance at the output can make the part unstable; at the input it forms a low-pass with the source impedance. Keep plane edges at the device away from the signal pins. Use low-reactance resistors (surface-mount best; metal-film or carbon-composition leaded parts also work), never wirewound. Short links to other wideband parts use 50 mil to 100 mil traces with the planes opened round them; a long run can be a matched microstrip or stripline, accepting the 6 dB loss of double termination. A higher-impedance environment than 50 Ω improves distortion. Solder the part down; a socket adds parasitics that spoil the response.

The part is built on a very high-speed complementary bipolar process with low junction breakdowns. Every pin has ESD diodes to both supplies, which also give moderate protection against inputs driven past the rails and typically carry 30 mA continuously. Where more current is possible (for example a ±15 V part driving the input), add series current-limiting resistors, kept as small as possible since large values hurt noise and bandwidth.

Typical line impedances are 240 Ω for symmetrical traces, 75 Ω or 50 Ω for coaxial cable, and as low as 30 Ω to 40 Ω for busses on PCBs; each high-impedance input on a daisy-chained line adds a few picofarads and lowers the impedance. A line normally carries a termination at its driving end and always at its receiving end; an unterminated line reflects the signal back and forth and the original can be lost.
A SPICE model predicts transient and small-signal frequency behaviour well, harmonic distortion and differential gain and phase less well, and makes no difference between the two packages.
